Colorado State.title: Mora's breaking point: What's really going on inside CSU football?
Colorado State.summary:
Following an embarrassing 31-14 loss at Utah State, Jim Mora unleashed a fiery postgame tirade unlike anything we've heard from a CSU head coach in years. He called out his players, coaching staff, the program's culture, and even the university itself, declaring that "the hammer is coming down." Joel and Mike dissect Mora's explosive comments, revisit the baffling decision to retain former defensive coordinator Tyson Summers, and explore whether deeper issues behind the scenes could be complicating CSU's rebuild. They also discuss Amy Parsons' surprising departure as university president, the questions surrounding CSU's commitment to athletics, and what all of this could mean for Mora's future in Fort Collins. Plus, a brief look ahead to a daunting matchup with Boise State and the start of CSU basketball season.

Colorado State.title: The Hauss is back! CSU wins a wild one, but can the Rams keep it rolling?
Colorado State.summary:
After four straight losses, CSU football finally gave fans something to celebrate with a thrilling 56-49 win over San Diego State. Joel and Mike break down the wild shootout, highlighted by Hauss Hejny's spectacular return from injury, accounting for 418 yards and five touchdowns. The guys discuss why Hejny is a game-changer, what CSU must do to keep him in Fort Collins beyond this season, and why this explosive offense makes Rams football more entertaining than it's been in years. The defense remains a mess, but timely turnovers and some improvement against the run helped secure the win. Plus, the guys look ahead to a Halloween road trip to Utah State, where another victory could put bowl eligibility back within reach, and briefly discuss CSU basketball's concerning exhibition loss at San Diego.

The guys break down the matchup, the Aztecs' vulnerabilities, and why Joel is surprisingly optimistic about CSU's chances. Plus, with bowl eligibility slipping away, what will it take to salvage the season and restore some confidence in the direction of the program?

Colorado State.title: A defensive disaster: CSU gets embarrassed on Homecoming, Tyson Summers is out
Colorado State.summary:
What should have been a celebration turned into another nightmare for CSU football. A record 41,000 fans packed Canvas Stadium for Homecoming and the Rams’ first Pac-12 conference game, only to watch Oregon State roll up 650 yards without punting once in a 56-26 rout. Joel and Mike break down another historically bad defensive performance before diving into the biggest story of the weekend: Jim Mora stripping defensive coordinator Tyson Summers of play-calling duties mid-game, Summers leaving the sideline, and his subsequent dismissal from the program. Was the change overdue? And, why did Mora allow the defense to reach this point in the first place? The guys examine Summers’ surprising retention from the previous staff, Mora’s own responsibility for CSU’s three-game collapse, and whether new play-caller Kenny McClendon can use the bye week to finally make this defense remotely competent.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's offensive execution falters down the stretch of LSU loss | Rewind
Gonzaga.summary:
There might be some apprehension from Gonzaga fans the next time the Bulldogs establish a double-digit lead against a marquee nonconference opponent.

Mark Few’s team escaped against Purdue in the season opener despite watching an 11-point lead shrivel away late in the second half.

Gonzaga appeared to be in even better shape on Saturday against LSU, going up by 13 points with 8 minutes, 11 seconds to play and maintaining an eight-point cushion with under three minutes left at Numerica Veterans Arena.

An avalanche of Gonzaga errors and tidal wave of LSU 3-pointers followed, allowing the Tigers to claw back and pull off a stunning upset on Donovan Dent’s clutch stepback 3 with 1.5 seconds remaining.

“Just a great win for us, you know, come back from 13 down with eight minutes left,” LSU coach Will Wade said. “Got to stay connected. I mean, this is the first time I’ve been up here. It’s an incredible atmosphere and the only thing I can compare it to when I was at VCU, but this is like VCU times five. Just to see the students and the buses pulled around this morning and the line was, I don’t even know how long it was, but they’re 190-9 up here.”

Now 190-10, as Wade astutely pointed out to LSU players in a postgame locker room video shared to the Tigers’ social media platforms.

Free-throw shooting, defensive rebounding and late-game offensive execution will all be on the to-do list for the 14th-ranked Zags, who figure to drop a few spots in Monday’s updated Associated Press poll.

We take another look at what went wrong and review some of the positives from Gonzaga’s first loss in our day-after rewind.

Closing time

It was an up-and-down game for Davis Fogle, one of Gonzaga’s most important players down the stretch two weeks earlier against Purdue.

Fogle registered two early steals against LSU, but missed his first four shots from the field and six of his first eight. The sophomore wing experienced lower-body cramps early in the second half and left the game for approximately four minutes before returning with 11:21 to go.

Fogle found an offensive rhythm, making his next four shots and converting two free throws to score nine points over a span of six minutes, but Gonzaga’s top scorer – and virtually every teammate – went ice-cold down the stretch, missing a jumper with 29 seconds left, coming up short on the back end of a 1-and-1 free throw set and missing a 40-foot heave at the buzzer.

“I think just coming back, just do whatever it took to win,” Fogle said. “I mean, they were playing great when I came back in, and then down the stretch, it’s kind of like (Braden Huff) said, there’s no excuse that we were tired. We got to come down with those rebounds and seal out the game.”

It’s likely Gonzaga will continue putting the ball in Fogle’s hands down the stretch of tight games. The Anacortes native is GU’s most versatile offensive option, the team’s top scorer at 19.7 ppg and generally reliable at the charity stripe. Fogle went 9 of 10 from the line against Purdue and 3 of 4 against New Mexico State before finishing 4 of 7 against LSU.

Making way for Wiggins

Chauncey Wiggins broke out a navy dress suit for his preliminary injunction hearing Thursday afternoon at Spokane County Courthouse. Two days later, Wiggins was dressed in a white No. 9 jersey, making his long-awaited Gonzaga debut after spending the last three months in eligibility limbo.

“He’s been a Zag throughout his whole process,” Fogle said, “so it’s awesome to finally get him out on the court with us, and he’s definitely going to find his stride and help us a lot as he did tonight.”

Wiggins subbed in at the 14:39 mark of the first half and pulled down two rebounds inside his first three minutes of action. The Florida State transfer missed his first two shots from the field, but connected on Gonzaga’s first 3-pointer of the game after eight consecutive misses.

“We’re happy he’s back and I think he’s going to be a big piece for us,” Huff said. “Now it’s just about getting his rhythm, finding his role and just figuring out all that stuff. But he’s going to be a good piece for us and we’re excited to have him playing with us.”

Wiggins finished with three points and three rebounds in 12 minutes. He was 1 of 3 from the field and 1 of 2 from the 3-point line. The veteran wing was on the floor in the final minutes and guarding Dent when LSU’s guard pulled up for the game-winning 3.

Unprompted, Wade brought up Wiggins in his postgame news conference after the LSU coach was asked about Tigers forward RJ Luis Jr., who recently earned an injunction from a Louisiana judge but didn’t travel with the team to Spokane.

“I can’t comment on that because we’re in litigation still,” he said. “But I will say this, I’m happy Wiggins got cleared. I know most coaches would be up here complaining. Wiggins should have played the first two games. I’ve talked to coach Few, we’ve had like weekly standing calls with all the eligibility stuff, but I’m thrilled for Wiggins. I’m glad that he was – not happy he hit the 3 on us – but I’m glad that he was able to get there.

“It’s just a shame that he had to miss two games and the exhibitions, and the exhibition game he missed against Arkansas was a high-level game – and he had to miss those games just because adults won’t do what the right thing is. It was great talking with the crowd, and the crowd’s reaction when he came in the game. Because it’s tough when these kids mentally get jerked around back and forth like that. But I’m happy that Wiggins was able to play and these are the eight we’re rolling with.”

High praise for Harwell

Fogle and Huff have paced Gonzaga from a scoring standpoint, but sophomore guard Isiah Harwell has quietly been one of the team’s top producers through three games.

Numerica Veterans Arena was anything but quiet when Harwell made a 3-pointer to break a 49-49 tie in the second half and erupted for the second time when the guard knocked down his second 3 to open up an eight-point Gonzaga lead with about 12 minutes to play.

Minutes before Fogle exited the game with cramps, Harwell took a hard shot to the chest on the defensive end of the floor. Few and athletic trainer Josh Therrien helped the guard off the floor, but he returned three minutes later.

“I thought he was really, really courageous,” Few said. “He really got the wind knocked out of him, I have to look at the play, but he was really, really hurting. But then to jump right back in there and make some huge kind of tough minded, really, veteran savvy kind of shots, I thought.”

Harwell, who had just three double-digit scoring performances last season at Houston, now has consecutive double-digit efforts with 22 points against NMSU and 14 against LSU. Behind Fogle and Huff, he’s GU’s third-leading scorer, averaging 12.7 ppg to go with 3.0 rpg.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women just miss upset as Stanford rallies for 67-65 win
Gonzaga.summary:
Considering the debacle two days earlier, the fact the Gonzaga women’s basketball team had the final shot to tie or win Sunday was a measurable stride in the right direction.

With no time but to catch and shoot, junior forward Lauren Whittaker’s attempt from 9 feet on the baseline, while being crowded by a 6-foot-4 defender, had no chance as the Stanford Cardinal rallied for a 67-65 win at Maples Pavilion in Palo Alto, California.

Whittaker made a 3-pointer with :06.3 remaining to pull Gonzaga within 66-65.

Stanford’s Hailee Swain made one of two foul shots with 5 seconds to go. As Gonzaga advanced the ball, Stanford (4-1) had a foul to give and the Cardinal fouled Allie Turner before she could set herself for a shot, leaving eight-tenths of a second on the clock.

With no timeouts, Gonzaga (2-3) got the ball to Whittaker, but she didn’t have a good look as time expired.

Gonzaga committed six of its 16 turnovers in the fourth quarter. Perhaps the deadliest miscue came with 1:56 remaining when Swain, on the ensuing possession, hit a 3-pointer to break a 62-62 tie.

“When we were patient our offense was pretty good,” GU coach Lisa Fortier said. “We got a little inpatient from time to time and that cost us, especially late.”

The loss overshadowed a nice bounce-back performance for three quarters following the Zags’ 82-62 loss at Grand Canyon on Friday.

Gonzaga trailed 13-12 early before piecing together a solid offensive stretch that saw the Zags finish the first quarter on an 11-2 surge for a 23-15 lead.

A basket from Ines Bettencourt gave the Zags their biggest lead, 25-15, early in the second.

Stanford fought back, pulling within 32-31 with 2:52 to go before halftime. But baskets from Whittaker and Taylor Smith gave Gonzaga a 36-32 lead at the break.

Back-to-back turnovers to open the second half opened the door for Stanford to pull even at 36-36. But five different players scored, capped by a basket from McKynnlie Dalan, as Gonzaga pushed ahead 46-41.

A 3-pointer from Teryn Gardner and a jumper from Zeryhia Aokuso extended Gonzaga’s lead to 54-45. Moments later, Whittaker took a good feed from Smith to put the Zags ahead 56-47.

But Stanford got a 3-pointer at the buzzer to go into the fourth quarter down 56-50.

Stanford, which has no seniors after getting hit hard in the transfer portal, took its first lead since the first quarter at 57-56.

The game would remain tight the rest of the way.

Whittaker had two big 3-pointers in the final 3:28.

Stanford had a seven-point advantage in points off turnovers.

The Zags played measurably better following the 82-62 loss at Grand Canyon on Friday.

“We did a much better job of competing,” Fortier said. “We had a nice game for most of it. We were playing together, we were playing hard on defense, we were making stuff happen.”

Gonzaga returns home Wednesday against Montana. Tipoff is at 6 p.m.

“There are tons of positives from the road trip,” Fortier said. “We’ve learned what we don’t want to be like and a little bit of what we do want to be like and what we are capable of. Hopefully that’s something we can continue to build and grow. Playing good teams on the road there’s always tons to learn. It teaches you about yourself and that’s why our schedule is how it is. So there’s lots of positives even though there weren’t wins in the win column.”

Turner led Gonzaga with 17 points and five assists. Whittaker had 16 points and six rebounds and Gardner added 10 points and four rebounds.

Stanford had four players in double figures led by Swain’s 20.

Gonzaga.title: LSU's Donovan Dent hits dagger 3 to complete 13-point comeback against Gonzaga
Gonzaga.summary:
LSU’s Donovan Dent ran red-hot in the first half, navigated an ice-cold stretch in the second and finished Gonzaga off with a stone-cold 3-pointer in the waning seconds of an exhilarating come-from-behind victory at Numerica Veterans Arena.

Gonzaga led by 13 points with 8 minutes, 11 seconds remaining when a late 3-point shooting flurry kickstarted LSU’s comeback. The Tigers connected on four 3’s in less than three minutes before Dent laced a 24-foot step-back shot over Chauncey Wiggins, instantly quieting a sellout crowd of 12,000 fans. A 45-foot heave from Davis Fogle ricocheted off the backboard as the buzzer sounded, sealing the first loss of the season for 14th-ranked Gonzaga and snapping a seven-game win streak at the Arena.

After corresponding with Dent about a potential move to Gonzaga this offseason, Mark Few’s team instead had to watch the fifth-year point guard post 23 points and dial up 10 assists in an LSU uniform. Dent scored 16 points in the first half but the UCLA transfer managed only four more in the second before the late 3-point dagger. Dent crossed halfcourt, stopping at the left wing before putting a dribble-move on Wiggins to create separation, giving him a clean look at the rim with less than five seconds on the game clock.

“My guy tripped at the halfcourt,” Dent said, describing the final play. “I was kind of giving it a running start momentum, so I’d get the pitch back. We got the switch and I don’t think we wanted to go to overtime here, so I knew I was shooting no matter what, and it went in.”

Dent, who planned to retire from basketball after the 2025-26 season, elected to pursue another season of eligibility late in the summer and touched base with Few’s coaching staff after Gonzaga lost starting point guard Mario Saint-Supery on July 11.

“It’s a great program. (Gonzaga) reached out to me, LSU reached out to me,” Dent said. “Ultimately I chose coach (Will) Wade and his staff, and I’m happy with it.”

Dent and the transfer point guard Gonzaga eventually signed, Florida’s Xaivian Lee, both won a preliminary injunction in California three months ago, clearing both to compete in 2026-27 and putting them on opposite ends of the court Saturday afternoon.

Lee picked up two fouls inside the first two minutes and was whistled for his third before halftime. Gonzaga’s starting point guard provided some clutch shooting in the second half, but also committed a costly turnover with 1 minute, 11 seconds left, traveling after he slipped on a sideline out-of-bounds play.

Gonzaga made a series of late mental mistakes, unraveling down the stretch of a game the Bulldogs appeared in firm control of when Braden Huff’s short jumper extended the lead to 68-55.

Gonzaga made 12 of 15 shots from the field at one point in the second half to build a double-digit lead, but finished 4 of 13 down the stretch and didn’t make a shot in the final three minutes.

Meanwhile, LSU settled into an offensive groove late in the game, making 8 of its final 12 shots while getting nine points on three 3-pointers from guard Abdi Bashir Jr. in the final 5 minutes, 20 seconds.

“Obviously we did lose shooters, some of it was the actions they were running,” Few said. “We have to tag on their bigs rolling, got a couple of guys miss the low hole so they had to cover in or give up a dunk. Then obviously just the offensive glass I thought was a key again. Just huge, huge offensive rebound after offensive rebound.

“We’d get a stop on the first action and then they’d just pin their ear back and we couldn’t get an offensive rebound at the end, including a huge one on a free throw, which we’ve worked on a lot.”

Bashir Jr. supplemented LSU’s scoring with 15 points on 5 of 8 shooting from the 3-point line for a Tigers team that finished 8 of 14 from distance in the second half.

Huff led Gonzaga with 18 points and 13 rebounds, finishing 8 of 16 from the field. Fogle overcame a slow offensive start and navigated lower-body cramps in the second half to finish with 15 points on 5-of-13 shooting, 1 of 5 from the 3-point line and 4 of 7 from the free throw line. Fogle also had eight rebounds and six assists. Shooting guard Isiah Harwell lifted Gonzaga’s offense in the second half with a pair of 3-pointers and finished with 14 points.

Gonzaga was 0 of 8 from deep before Wiggins made the team’s first 3-pointer with 17 minutes, 35 seconds remaining in the second half. Wiggins, who secured a fifth year of eligibility Thursday afternoon through a preliminary injunction in Spokane Country, had three points in 13 minutes for Gonzaga.

Gonzaga.title: No offense to LSU – or Gonzaga – but there has to be a better path forward in age of NIL | Ralph Walter
Gonzaga.summary:
Moments after Gonzaga and LSU tipped off Saturday afternoon at Numerica Veterans Arena, Zags player No. 5 used a nifty move to drive past his man and hit a short jumper for the game’s first basket. A bit later, No. 2 pressed full-court, stole the ball and fed a streaking No. 13 for a two-handed slam that sent the packed house into a frenzy.

My apologies, still putting names with faces – and numbers.

In a bruising game that matched the Zags’ seven veteran transfers – along with holdovers Braden Huff and Davis Fogle – against a talented Tigers team boasting even more seasoned newcomers, it was 22-year-old ex-UCLA guard Donovan Dent who drilled a 3-pointer with a second left to beat 14th-ranked GU, 81-80.

With its electric atmosphere, stomping student section and unmistakable championship intensity, Saturday’s contest felt like most big Gonzaga games.

So why does it all feel so empty?

Is it because the college game has devolved into 20-something rentals battling fellow 20-something rentals? Or maybe the endless roster shakeups that have left fans feeling like they don’t know any players anymore? Perhaps it’s the greed-fueled dissolution of traditional leagues and rivalries? Or is it that we seem to spend more time following eligibility proceedings in courts rather than action on them?

Whatever the reasons, college athletics – specifically basketball and football – seem broken.

To be fair, this is much bigger than Gonzaga vs. LSU. It’s happening all across the nation, at all levels.

But Saturday’s game at the Arena offered more proof that college sports have lost their way.

Combined, the GU and LSU rosters reportedly earn somewhere north of $30 million. The average age of the Tigers’ starting five is slightly higher than what the San Antonio Spurs trotted out during the NBA playoffs last spring.

Controversial LSU coach Will Wade, who returned this season after the school fired him for alleged NCAA infractions in 2022, added three players with international professional experience and seven college transfers who have combined to play at 21 different schools. That doesn’t include RJ Luis, who spent the past year and a half away from the college game and seemed destined to remain ineligible because of SEC rules. He was granted a preliminary injunction on Friday, and according to social media tried unsuccessfully to catch a plane for Spokane in time to join his teammates. Luis, who began his career at UMass, played two seasons for St. John’s from 2023-25. He eventually played in three NBA preseason games with the Boston Celtics in 2025 before getting cut. He’ll be 24 in two weeks.

Wade has been steadfast in his recruiting approach, saying in September, “We’re going to be unapologetic. This is who we are. This is what we’re doing.”

Gonzaga’s path to fifth-year transfers hasn’t entirely been its own doing. GU’s returning core of Braden Huff, Davis Fogle and Mario Saint-Supery from last season were all original Zag recruits. But Saint-Supery bolted for a Spanish professional team in July, and heralded German recruit Jack Kayil chose to forgo Spokane for the NBA draft.

Those late departures further pushed coach Mark Few and his staff into the “5-in-5” pool, where they landed Xaivian Lee, Javon Bennett and Chauncey Wiggins, three players who are each playing for their third school. Wiggins, who became eligible on Thursday, played three games for the Boston Celtics at Summer League in July.

GU added two other transfers: Nathan De Sousa, a senior on his last year of eligibility whose resumé includes five seasons playing professionally in France; and junior Izan Almansa, who’s played three seasons of professional basketball, most recently for Real Madrid after not hearing his name called in the 2025 NBA draft.

Against LSU, several of the first-year Zags had their moments in a game that saw GU surrender a 13-point, second-half lead. Isiah Harwell, the sophomore transfer from Houston, scored 14 points, Almansa had eight points and seven rebounds, and the pesky Bennett came off the bench to provide six points and five assists.

On paper, this Gonzaga roster is big, deep and primed to make another deep NCAA run.

But at what cost? College basketball has nothing to do with college now. It’s hard to imagine any of these guys actually showing up to class or interacting with fellow students at College Hall.

School loyalty used to mean something. But it’s severely one-sided at the moment, with fans paying more and more to watch players – and coaches – come and go at the bounce of a ball. Two nosebleeds to Saturday’s game were going for well over 100 bucks.

This here-today, gone-tomorrow approach is taking a toll. CBS Sports reported that in 2025-26 only 22 scholarship seniors across the power conferences spent their entire careers where they started.

These new Zags all seem like good guys. They’re obviously talented and will win plenty of games. And their coach has showed loyalty, staying in Spokane for decades while richer programs came-a-calling.

But being a fan in 2026 feels hollow, like we’re only cheering on the jersey without knowing the player wearing it.

Even with NIL and the transfer portal, it doesn’t have to be this way.

A year ago, Michigan State’s Tom Izzo was quoted as saying, “When I go in the portal, the first place I go is my locker room. I want to keep most of the guys on my team.”

Izzo’s Spartans, who are 4-0 and ranked No. 5, returned nearly everyone from a season ago, picking up just one transfer while losing another one.

That was always the Gonzaga way. Over the years we watched as raw freshmen developed into true Zags – the Ronny Turiafs, the Steven Grays, the Corey Kisperts, the Anton Watsons. Braden Huff and Davis Fogle are following that tradition. Maybe a couple of current GU freshmen still stick around long enough to make that same leap in the coming years.

At least that’s what we ought to be rooting for.

Otherwise, as Jerry Seinfeld once said about professional sports, we’re just rooting for laundry.

Gonzaga.title: Donovan Dent's clutch shots help Tigers upset Bulldogs | Difference makers
Gonzaga.summary:
Offensive difference maker: Through the first 20 minutes, the best player on the court was unquestionably LSU guard Donovan Dent. The fifth-year transfer from UCLA scored 16 points in the opening half, including a banked-in 3-pointer at the halftime buzzer to give LSU a 2-point lead at the break. Dent was much more quiet in the second half, scoring just four points before hitting the afternoon’s biggest shot – a game-winning 3-pointer with 1.5 seconds remaining. Dent – a transfer target of Gonzaga this summer – finished with 23 points and 10 assists.

Defensive difference maker: It took just 1 minute, 45 seconds for Gonzaga starting point guard Xaivian Lee to pick up a pair of personal fouls, forcing Gonzaga coach Mark Few to turn to his bench and reserve guard Javon Bennett. The fifth-year Dayton transfer took advantge of the opportunity and was a menace on the defensive end of the floor for the Zags, nabbing four steals and dishing our five assists in his 23 minutes of action.

Key moment: With the Bulldogs up by two points with 12 seconds remaining, Gonzaga guard Davis Fogle missed the back-end of a 1-and-1, giving LSU and Dent the ball back with a chance to go for the tie or win. Dent got isolated on newly-eligible Gonzaga wing Chauncey Wiggins on the perimeter and hit a 25-foot triple over Wiggins’ outstretched arms to secure the upset for LSU.

Gonzaga.title: Donovan Dent's jumper gives LSU win over No. 14 Gonzaga | Recap and highlights
Gonzaga.summary:
Donovan Dent hit a step-back 3-pointer with 1.5 seconds remaining as LSU stormed back from as many as 13 points down in the second half to stun No. 14 Gonzaga 81-80 on Saturday in front of a packed crowd at Numerica Veterans Arena.

Dent — a Gonzaga transfer target this offseason — paced the Tigers (4-0) with 23 points, while fellow guards Abdi Bashir Jr. and Skyy Clark added 15 and 14 points apiece.

Braden Huff led the Zags (2-1) with a double-double of 18 points and 13 rebounds, while Davis Fogle had 15 points for GU. Sophomore transfer guard Isiah Harwell added 14 points for GU, including a pair of momentum-shifting 3-pointers in the second half to help guide GU to its initial double-digit cushion.

Gonzaga trailed midway through the contest 39-37 after Dent scored 16 first-half points for the Tigers. But the Bulldogs finally got the offense on track in the second half, starting with a 3-pointer from newly-eligible wing Chauncey Wiggins at the 17:35 mark of the half. Wiggins’ 3-pointer was the first make of the day from deep for GU, which went 0-8 in the first half. Gonzaga shot 53.3% from the floor in the second half.

On the defensive end, backup point guard Javon Bennett was disruptive for the Zags, finishing with four steals and five assists. Bennett was forced into extra minutes after starting guard Xaivian Lee picked up two fouls in the game’s opening two minutes.

Forward Izan Almanasa also played key minutes off the bench for GU, finishing with eight points and seven rebounds while playing most of the second half in place of starting forward Massamba Diop — who was limited to seven points in 22 minutes.

The Zags finished shooting 44.6% from the floor and 29.4% from 3-point range, while LSU shot 43.1% overall and 46.2% from deep. The Bulldogs also forced 13 LSU turnovers.

Gonzaga returns home Tuesday to take on Montana State at 8 p.m. — GU’s last game before heading to Las Vegas for the Players Era Festival over Thanksgiving.

Gonzaga.title: Donovan Dent, LSU guards leave an impression on Zags; Javon Bennett solid off bench | 3 takeaways
Gonzaga.summary:
Three takeaways from Gonzaga’s 81-80 loss to LSU on Saturday at Numerica Veterans Arena.

Tigers guards come through

LSU’s backcourt was a handful throughout for the Zags, even before UCLA transfer Donovan Dent delivered a dagger 3-pointer with one second remaining.

Gonzaga threatened to pull away in the second half, taking a 68-55 lead with 8:11 left, but the Tigers stayed within striking range behind a trio of guards.

Skyy Clark, who entered the game just 1 of 16 on 3-pointers, hit three 3s. Clark, also a UCLA transfer, tallied a season-high 14 points. Abdi Bashir Jr. nailed four second-half 3s, all seemingly at timely moments in the final 12 minutes, and finished with 15 points.

Dent swished a game-winning 3 over Chauncey Wiggins to send the Tigers home with an upset win.

Add in Divine Ogochukwu’s seven points and LSU’s four guards combined for 59 of LSU’s 81 points.

The Tigers led 39-37 at half, largely due to Dent’s 16 points, including a banked-in 3-pointer just before the buzzer.

Bennett big off bench

Gonzaga got into early foul trouble when starting point guard Xaivian Lee picked up two quick fouls, but Javon Bennett came through with quality minutes in both halves.

Bennett scored on a layup with 16:06 left for just GU’s second field goal. He snagged three steals, two leading to transition baskets, and added an assist and a pair of free throws in 13 first-half minutes.

Bennett had another shift late in the half when Lee picked up his third foul with 3:50 remaining. Gonzaga held the lead for 13 of 20 first-half minutes.

Bennett continued to be effective in the closing half as the Zags stretched their lead. He fed Isiah Harwell for a corner 3-pointer after an LSU turnover. Harwell’s bucket put Gonzaga on top 59-51 with 11:47 remaining.

The same combination – Bennett dish, Harwell jam – connected a few minutes later to push Gonzaga’s lead to nine.

Bennett finished with six points, five assists and four steals.

Lee contributed nine points and two assists in 13 minutes.

Wiggins debuts

Chauncey Wiggins, the Florida State transfer who became eligible Thursday after being granted a temporary injunction by Spokane Superior Court Judge Dean Chuang, immediately joined GU’s rotation.

He subbed in with 14:38 left in the first half. The 6-foot-11 forward didn’t score in 4½ minutes, but he responded in the second half with a 3-ball shortly after entering the game to give GU a 43-41 lead.

Wiggins had three points and three boards in 12 minutes.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Braden Huff battles inside for 18 points, 13 boards in loss to LSU
Gonzaga.summary:
Braden Huff has never had more rebounds in a Gonzaga game.

He collected 13 against LSU on Saturday at Numerica Veterans Arena, four more than the senior’s previous high, but he, like his teammates, was left wanting more, especially in crunch time.

The visiting Tigers caught and passed Gonzaga with a 10-1 closing run. Donovan Dent capped it with a 3-pointer with 1 second left in LSU’s 81-80 upset victory, stunning a packed house.

LSU’s offensive rebounding in the second half played a major role in its ability to stay in the game and ultimately rally from a 68-55 deficit. Exactly one-third of the Tigers’ second-half points, 14 of 42, came after offensive boards, a category Gonzaga dominated in the opening half.

“That’s not an excuse, especially that late in the game. You have to find your legs, it’s winning time,” said Huff, who logged 36 minutes, matching his season high vs. Purdue. “We’ve got to be more physical, more tough, limit them to one shot. Limit them to one shot it’s a different story and we’re a lot happier.”

Huff gave GU that 68-55 lead with 8:11 left with a soft-touch basket in the lane for the last of his 18 points. He operated with his typical effectiveness against LSU’s stout frontcourt, creating space with back-down post moves and finishing in the paint. He was 8 of 14 before missing his last two shots.

“He’s a load, I love 13 (Izan Almansa) as well,” LSU coach Will Wade said. “I thought they played (Almansa) more than (Massamba) Diop in the second half just because of the ball-screen D, you’d have to ask coach (Mark) Few, and just his physicality.”

Wade last faced GU when he was the head coach at McNeese. He chose to double team Gonzaga’s frontcourt, led by Graham Ike and Anton Watson, in the Zags’ 86-65 first-round win in the 2024 NCAA Tournament.

Ike didn’t miss a shot and scored 16 points while Watson hung 13 points, 13 rebounds and nine assists on the Cowboys. Huff chipped in seven points in 16 minutes coming off the bench.

“We brought two people to all those guys and they just cut us up on the back side,” Wade recalled. “So (Saturday) we just tried to let them back us down and keep everybody attached so they didn’t get the cut with (Davis) Fogle and the other guys sneaking underneath.”

“Huff is just a great player and he backed us down and scored enough, but we had enough resistance down there a few times that we were able to stop him. But he’s a phenomenal player.”

Huff did some damage with his six offensive rebounds. He scored on a pair of putbacks after Fogle misses in the first half. Huff scored 10 of his 18 points in the second half and he grabbed a couple of defensive rebounds during the Tigers’ comeback.

Huff, held without a rebound in 25 minutes in Gonzaga’s win over New Mexico State last Saturday, led the Zags in defensive (seven) and offensive (six) boards. LSU freshman Michael Ruzic was the only other player with double-digit rebounds (12).

None of that mattered to the senior forward after the Zags’ eight-point lead melted away in the final 3 minutes.

“They’re a physical team,” Huff said. “We knew we had to be physical. Thirteen boards is cool, but at the end of the game we have to get some of those and close it out.

“Just have to find a way to win and just figure it out.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Davis Fogle to face stern defensive test from LSU, Saliou Niang | Key matchup
Gonzaga.summary:
Davis Fogle eventually hopes to test his game at the highest level, with NBA aspirations that could materialize sooner rather than later for the Gonzaga wing.

Fogle could get some early experience on that front Saturday when he matches up against an LSU player who was not only coveted by NBA front offices but actually drafted by one of them in 2025.

In a sequence of events that would’ve been hard to fathom for hoops players even two years ago, Saliou Niang was selected No. 58 overall by the Cleveland Cavaliers and played three games for the Eastern Conference franchise at Las Vegas Summer League before bypassing NBA and G League opportunities to sign with Virtus Bologna of Italy’s Lega Basket Serie A.

A year later, Niang matriculated into college basketball, signing with coach Will Wade and the LSU team visiting Numerica Veterans Arena for a 12:30 p.m. (USA Network) matchup with No. 14 Gonzaga.

In all likelihood, it’ll be LSU’s best individual defender matched up with Gonzaga’s top scorer when the teams tip off early Saturday afternoon.

Of LSU’s starters, the 6-foot-8 Niang is the most logical choice to guard the 6-foot-7 Fogle, Gonzaga’s leading scorer through two games and the Pac-12 Offensive Player of the Week after he posted consecutive 22-point performances against Purdue and New Mexico State.

“It’s huge, he can guard everywhere, he can guard one through five,” Wade said of Niang after the team’s season-opening win over LSU New Orleans. “He’s just a monster defender and just a really, really good player. A really, really good all-around player, but just to have somebody with his versatility and his athleticism is really important.”

The 22-year-old Niang will be the best defensive player Fogle’s encountered this season, and possibly since he arrived at Gonzaga. Fogle, meanwhile, should be a serious test for Niang after the Tigers pocketed three comfortable wins against overmatched opponents from LSU New Orleans, Texas Southern and Louisiana Tech.

Fogle will have to be mindful handling the ball when face-guarded by Niang. The athletic junior is averaging 3.3 steals and registered six in the season opener against New Orleans. Niang has also been a key to LSU’s transition offense, attacking the glass for defensive rebounds before quickly pushing ahead to guards Donovan Dent and Skyy Clark. In addition to his 11.7 points per game, Niang is averaging 10.3 rebounds and 3.7 assists.

“He’s a great defensive rebounder,” Wade said. “He got nine defensive rebounds (against LSU New Orleans) and he pushed the ball out two or three dribbles. That gets your break going. Sal’s probably our second-best passer to Donny (Dent). Sal’s really, really solid there. Him being able to grab those defensive rebounds and push the ball out is certainly helpful for us on the offensive side.”

Niang’s defensive assignment becomes more interesting when the Zags insert newly-eligible wing Chauncey Wiggins into the lineup, likely sliding Fogle to the ‘2.’ That could give GU a matchup advantage at multiple positions, forcing the 6-2 Clark to defend the 6-7 Fogle and placing the 6-8 Niang on the 6-11 Wiggins.

Gonzaga.title: No. 14 Gonzaga welcomes reconstructed LSU team for big nonconference showdown: 'They've got a heckuva roster'
Gonzaga.summary:
Mark Few isn’t in the business of ranking college basketball teams, but there’d be at least one or two key discrepancies between a hypothetical poll created by Gonzaga’s coach and the Associated Press version assembled by media members every week throughout the regular season.

For one, there wouldn’t be many teams listed higher than the LSU squad traveling to Spokane this Saturday for a 12:30 p.m. (USA Network) nonconference matchup against Gonzaga at Numerica Veterans Arena.

The unranked Tigers (3-0) still aren’t collecting AP votes two weeks into Will Wade’s second stint with the SEC schools, but they have Few’s undivided attention and then some heading into Saturday’s high-profile game against the 14th-ranked Zags (2-0).

“I’m telling you, he’s got a heckuva roster now,” Few said. “Might not be as talented as Duke, but it’s probably the second-most talented roster maybe in college basketball with who they have. I don’t think everybody knows the level of play of the kids they got from the international ranks. They’re something.”

National skepticism around LSU probably stems from a few different sources. The Tigers have obliterated three opponents to this point, handling LSU New Orleans 100-57, Texas Southern 92-51 and Louisiana Tech 90-50, but still haven’t played anyone ranked higher than No. 264 at KenPom.

As Wade put it in a press conference earlier this week, the Tigers are “jumping into the deep end” with Saturday’s game against a Gonzaga team ranked No. 11 at KenPom.

The Tigers arrived in Spokane from Baton Rouge, La., on Thursday night and weren’t impacted by Friday’s nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that disrupted games around the country.

“I think I was the only one dumb enough to go up there and play them,” Wade said. “They tried to get everyone else and we were the only ones dumb enough to sign up for it. It’s going to be one of the biggest challenges of our entire season when you look at our schedule. So great program, Hall of Fame coach and they’ve got great personnel.”

LSU’s personnel, meanwhile, is more of an unknown.

After hiring Wade from North Carolina State, the Tigers didn’t bring back a single player from their 2025-26 team and the coach’s unique roster-building tactics became a popular talking point during college basketball’s offseason.

Wade added multiple 5-in-5 guards from the UCLA team that lost to Gonzaga in Seattle last year – Donovan Dent and Skyy Clark – signed forward Saliou Niang, the 58th overall pick of the 2025 NBA Draft, and brought in 23-year-old center Brice Dessert, who has extensive experience playing overseas and in the EuroLeague.

LSU’s coach also drew criticism for signing former St. John’s standout and Big East Player of the Year RJ Luis, who signed a two-way contract with the Utah Jazz after going undrafted in 2025. The Tigers initially chose not to put Luis on their roster after the SEC introduced rules related to NBA Draft declarations and signed contracts, but a Louisiana judge recently granted a preliminary injunction to the forward, ordering that LSU roster him according to multiple media outlets Friday afternoon.

Luis made an attempt to join the team in Spokane for Saturday’s game, but wasn’t able to travel Friday due to the flight outages, according to Matt Moscona of the After Further Review show.

The Zags picked from many of the same player pools to fill their roster, adding 5-in-5 transfers Xaivian Lee, Javon Bennett and Chauncey Wiggins – the latter of which received an injunction on Thursday, allowing him to debut against LSU. Gonzaga also signed two international pros: forward Izan Almansa and point guard Nathan De Sousa. Almansa was sidelined for a 109-68 victory over New Mexico State with a sore calf but could return to play LSU.

“He’s adapted to this current state of college basketball as good as any,” Few said of Wade. “We’ve talked about obviously having guys in the California case, we’ve talked about that and we were both frustrated with the delays and the length, we had no idea what was going on with the internationals, which is something that hasn’t really been reported.

“When you have to wait all the way until November before you find out who’s eligible and all our players were the type that were eligible the year before. So kind of all this is tied together and the fact he was proactive about it and went out.”

After being terminated by LSU in 2022 for recruiting allegations and his involvement in a FBI wiretap investigation, Wade landed on his feet two years later at McNeese State, matching up with Gonzaga in a No. 5 vs. No. 12 matchup in the 2024 NCAA Tournament. The Zags overpowered the Cowboys in the paint and controlled the glass, cruising to an 86-65 opening-round victory.

“They’re going to pound that thing into the paint,” Wade said. “They’re a sight to behold when you play them. … The tape doesn’t do justice of their transition offense and just how physical their bigs are. It’ll be a monumental challenge for us, just the way they build their team. They’ve got a great shooter with (Davis) Fogle, so they’ve got some really, really good team. Their pieces and parts fit really, really well.”

The Zags will also have the backing of a home crowd. Gonzaga has won seven consecutive games at Numerica Veterans Arena dating back to a 2011 loss to Memphis, haven’t played a single-digit game during that stretch and have won four of the seven by at least 20 points.

“I know this, we’re getting money for our NIL for going up there, so the check ain’t going to bounce,” Wade said. “So that may be the best part of Saturday, because they’re going to put so many people in that arena. … Now our school’s taking 15% from us, which I’ve never heard of before. We are getting paid a good amount of money for going up there, because nobody else would go.”

Gonzaga.title: Turnover-prone Gonzaga women rolled by Grand Canyon 82-62
Gonzaga.summary:
It was over by halftime for the Gonzaga women’s basketball team Friday.

Without a doubt, Grand Canyon, picked to finish second in the Mountain West, is a solid team. The Antelopes were coming off a big win over Big Ten-Oregon.

But Gonzaga made the Antelopes look unbeatable thanks to 14 turnovers in the opening 20 minutes and allowing Grand Canyon to make 9 of 19 from 3-point range.

The final result had Grand Canyon cruising to a 82-62 win at Global Credit Union Arena in Phoenix.

It’d be tempting to say the game Friday was an aberration for Gonzaga – if it hadn’t been for last week’s loss to Idaho.

The Zags found themselves trailing Idaho 54-34 in their first loss. The first half against GCU felt worse.

GCU used a 15-0 run that spilled over from the first quarter to build a 31-18 lead. Gonzaga was scoreless in the second quarter until Lauren Whittaker made a basket while being fouled at the 5:49 mark.

Gonzaga (2-2) cut the lead under double digits at 31-23. But the Antelopes (3-0) finished the half on a 12-0 surge.

The Zags led 18-16 with 34 seconds left in the first quarter when Taylor Smith hit a jumper. Gonzaga stumbled measurably thereafter.

“I like the way we started the game … we didn’t have the same level of execution on the defensive side nor the offensive side in the second quarter,” GU coach Lisa Fortier said.

The nine made 3-pointers for GCU in the first half matched what the Antelopes made against Oregon.

GCU finished 17 of 32 from 3-point range and 28 of 60 from the field overall. Gonzaga, which led the nation in 3-point made efficiency last year, was 5 of 23 from distance and 21 of 59 overall.

The Zags finished with a season-high 22 turnovers.

It went from bad to worse early in the third quarter. GCU opened the period with a 10-0 run, and Gonzaga didn’t score until the 4:40 mark.

Gonzaga allowed Chloe Mann to go uncontested coast-to-coast for a layup at the buzzer to end the third, giving the Antelopes their biggest lead at 68-32.

The Zags showed some life in the fourth quarter. They trimmed GCU’s lead to 19 points.

“Unfortunately we allowed our struggles defensively to affect us offensively, which is what we’re trying to overcome at all times,” Fortier said. “I keep thinking that we’re more like the first and fourth quarter team. In my mind I envision us having those 25- to 30-point quarters and less like the team that has a seven-point quarter.”

Junior forward Lauren Whittaker led Gonzaga with 16 points and eight rebounds. Zeryhia Aokuso had 12 points and Teryn Gardner added 10.

Gonzaga has much to figure out. The video from the loss won’t cover up any truth. The Zags have struggled in both losses to defensive pressure, and they’re shooting poorly.

“So when things are hard, who are we going to be,” Fortier said. “When (other teams are), how are we going to make that stop. When we can’t score, where are we going to look to get that bucket that you can count on every single time. Those are all things we have to learn about our team. They are fixable. We’re going to have plenty of opportunities to fix them because our schedule is really hard. We’re going to continue to be tested. Four games in our only job is to learn and get better. I’m hoping we can learn some things from this and put it towards our game on Sunday.”

Gonzaga travels to Stanford on Sunday. Tipoff is at 2 p.m.

Tara VanDeveer Court will be a difficult place for the Zags to find some footing.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Chauncey Wiggins earns preliminary injunction, set to debut against LSU
Gonzaga.summary:
Expressionless for more than an hour, Chauncey Wiggins finally exhaled, closing his eyes as he tilted his head back and processed four months of emotions.

“Really just took a deep breath and said, ‘Thank you, God,’ about 20 times,” Wiggins said.

Spokane Superior Court Judge Dean Chuang granted a temporary injunction to the Gonzaga forward on Thursday afternoon - a ruling that allows Wiggins to suit up for the 14th-ranked Bulldogs this season and, by all accounts, signals the end of a roller-coaster eligibility saga for the 6-foot-11 transfer.

Wiggins, who was ineligible for season-opening wins over Purdue and New Mexico State last week, said he expects to debut for Gonzaga on Saturday in a high-profile nonconference matchup with LSU (12:30 p.m., USA Network) at Numerica Veterans Arena, just a few-hundred yards from the fourth-floor courtroom where the player’s injunction hearing took place Thursday.

“I had a lot of faith, a lot of positivity,” Wiggins said. “That’s how I live my life, so I was just really hopeful and very positive of the attorneys and lawyers and the judge. So I’m just really thankful for everybody.”

More than two-dozen people attended Wiggins’ afternoon hearing, including Gonzaga coach Mark Few and teammates Braden Huff, Davis Fogle, Xaivian Lee, Javon Bennett, Parker Jefferson and Alonzo Metz. Wiggins wasn’t scheduled to appear in court until next Tuesday, but with Saturday’s Gonzaga-LSU matchup in mind, the player’s attorneys filed for a motion to shorten time, moving the hearing up by five days.

Wiggins maintained an optimistic outlook, even at points when the 21-year-old’s chances of obtaining a fifth season appeared grim.

After playing three years at Clemson and spending the 2025-26 season at Florida State, Wiggins joined the Boston Celtics at NBA Summer League but didn’t sign a professional contract, allowing him to explore fifth-year eligibility options. Around the same time, dozens of athletes across different states and sports - including Gonzaga’s Lee and Bennett - filed lawsuits against the NCAA, claiming they should be entitled to a fifth year of competition through the regulatory body’s new 5-in-5 eligibility model.

Wiggins initially joined the Godfrey v. NCAA lawsuit in his home state of Georgia - a 5-in-5 case originally filed by former Clemson teammate and current Arizona forward RJ Godfrey. A Cobb County judge granted an injunction to the plaintiffs, but the Court of Appeals stayed the case, reversing the decision and keeping Wiggins ineligible. Wiggins bailed on the Georgia lawsuit when oral arguments were scheduled for Jan. 12, 2027 - effectively sidelining the forward through Gonzaga’s first 15 games - and joined the Wheeler v. NCAA 5-in-5 lawsuit based in Waco, Texas, hoping for a better outcome.

It ultimately backfired when a McLennan County judge ruled Wiggins and other new plaintiffs had “a lack of personal jurisdiction” in the suit, denying the request for a temporary restraining order one day after Gonzaga’s Nov. 2 opener against Purdue.

That brought Wiggins’ eligibility battle to Spokane for a third, and possibly final, shot at an injunction.

Chuang, a Gonzaga Law graduate, listened to arguments from Wiggins’ attorney, Ryan Downton of the Texas Trial Group, and NCAA attorneys David Zeitlin and Taylor Askew - all three of whom appeared virtually via Zoom.

A crux of Downton’s argument pertained to the NCAA Manual and language of a specific bylaw that doesn’t explicitly state class of 2022 high school graduates are excluded from the 5-in-5 model.

“If it was truly an error that the manual was supposed to exclude these athletes, then they would’ve gotten together with their Cabinet, they would’ve taken a vote on it and they would’ve voted to change the language of the manual,” Downton said. “… They haven’t done that and what you’re left with is unambiguous text that makes Mr. Wiggins eligible.”

Arguing on behalf of the NCAA, Askew claimed “everybody has to be operating under the same set of standards,” and argued that while dozens of fifth-year athletes are currently competing under injunctions, “that doesn’t mean it’s fair.”

The defense also raised concerns about equity and opportunities eliminated by allowing class of 2022 graduates to return for a fifth season. Askew specifically referenced controversy surrounding North Carolina’s women’s field hockey team, which had a losing record before three fifth-year players were granted midseason injunctions, allowing the Tar Heels to win three of their last four contests and claim a spot in the NCAA Tournament, subsequently knocking ACC rival Wake Forest out of the bracket.

“That’s not fair,” Askew said. “These players are playing with an advantage. These teams are playing with an advantage that their competitors do not have and that’s not how sports work.”

Wiggins sat patiently next to Spokane-based attorney Andrew Wagley, later admitting to the nerves and anxiety he felt as Downton and Askew went back and forth with arguments.

“My heart was beating every second of it, but I just tried to stay positive,” he said. “Shout out to Ryan, he did an amazing job. That’s probably the most locked in I’ve been listening to anybody. You know at school, those teachers be talking, but I was very locked in like, we got this, we got this.”

After 50 minutes of arguments from both sides, Chuang called for a 15-minute intermission and handed down the injunction order shortly after the hearing resumed. Citing a shortage of judicial officers, Chuang couldn’t schedule trial until May 10, 2027, meaning Wiggins’ case wouldn’t be heard until one month after Gonzaga’s season ended, at the earliest. As part of the ruling, Chuang also restrained the NCAA from enforcing the rule of restitution, meaning the governing body won’t be able to retroactively strip Gonzaga of victories or postseason awards while Wiggins is on the court.

Wiggins broke into a smile when the hearing ended and quickly found his teammates, trading hugs with all six in attendance before the group exited the courtroom.

“Those are my brothers. I’m just happy they came and supported me,” Wiggins said. “I transferred here for a reason, to win, and it’s just showing that off-the-court chemistry we have.”

Even as eligibility restrictions prevented him competing against Purdue and New Mexico State, Wiggins was able to establish some semblance of chemistry on the court through practices since arriving in Spokane two months ago.

“I’m very excited,” Wiggins said. “I’ve been waiting for this opportunity ever since I knew I could come back to college, so I’m just ready to play Saturday and play for the rest of the year.”

What exactly are the Zags getting from the newly-eligible wing? An extremely-capable outside shooter, for one. Wiggins made 72 total 3-pointers last season at FSU - 24 more than anyone on Gonzaga’s roster - and connected at a 38.7% clip from behind the arc while averaging 13.3 points per game.

“Just expect everything, expect us to win and expect some of my 3-pointers because I know everybody’s looking for that,” Wiggins said.

The experienced wing is a proven winner who played on Clemson teams that combined to go 74-30 between 2022-25 before starring on a Florida State team that went 18-15 in coach Luke Loucks’ first season and declined an invitation to the NIT.

“I’m really just looking to play, just to win, show my skillset,” Wiggins said. “Really just win, stay positive and just having faith out there on the court. I’m just very glad I got this opportunity.”

Gonzaga.title: LSU beat writer discusses coach Will Wade, Tigers keys vs. Gonzaga | Q&A
Gonzaga.summary:
LSU’s roster construction was in the national spotlight during the offseason as the program waited on eligibility waivers, court rulings and NCAA clearance on international standouts.

The talented Tigers might remain in the spotlight during the season as a force in the SEC and beyond.

LSU has averaged 94 points per game with a 41.3-point margin of victory in blowouts over three overmatched opponents.

The Tigers, picked No. 14 in the 16-team SEC preseason poll, have climbed to No. 27 in KenPom’s rankings after starting out at 47. Gonzaga, which faces LSU on Saturday at the Spokane Arena, checks in at No. 11.

We connected with Toyloy Brown III, who covers LSU for the Advocate newspaper based in Baton Rouge, for a closer look at the Tigers.

Q: At one point in late September, LSU’s official roster listed just four players, but coach Will Wade remained optimistic throughout that the roster would eventually take shape.

Now that the roster is largely set, highlight a player or two that will be crucial to the Tigers’ season.

Brown: Donovan Dent is essential for LSU to reach its ceiling. The 6-foot-2 point guard epitomizes what it means to be a floor general with his elite court vision and creativity as a playmaker. He remains poised under heavy defensive pressure, posting a 25-to-3 assist-to-turnover ratio thus far.

Dent has been just as electric on defense as an ideal fit for the high-pressure defense LSU employs. He isn’t only averaging over three steals per game, but also leads the team with 2.3 blocks, an underrated trait from his time at his previous stops.

LSU 7-footer Michael Ruzic has been remarkable despite coming off the bench. The 20-year-old from Croatia came to college with a reputation as a tall shooter. He started his collegiate career with an added 15 pounds to his now 235-pound frame that has complemented his skill as a finisher.

He has made an incredible 29 of 30 shots in the paint. His rim protection without fouling and overall awareness have also been better than expected early.

Q: Guessing this isn’t the first or last time you’ll be asked this: What is it like covering LSU coach Will Wade as a beat writer?

Brown: A Wade press conference is never boring. It’s hard for me to imagine there being many more college coaches as unfiltered. He is almost too quotable. If I include all the fun things he says, all my stories would be 1,000 words. I also have to be ready to record video at a moment’s notice. You never know when he’ll joke that NIL stands for “now it’s legal.”

The only not-so-fun part of covering Wade was the mystery of who is or will be on the team and when or if they’ll be eligible. Only four rotation players were certain to play before the season opener. Other than that, it has been a fun ride.

Q: LSU has stomped three overmatched opponents to open the season. Your takeaways of the team’s strengths/weaknesses thus far?

Brown: LSU did what it was supposed to do: crush teams with inferior talent. It did so in historic fashion, winning three straight games by 40 or more points for the first time. Its latest 40-point win over Louisiana Tech was the most impressive since KenPom’s model predicted only a 22-point win.

One strength has been the defensive intensity. The full-court and half-court pressure Wade’s team is playing with has bothered opponents even more than anticipated. Players like Dent and starting small forward Saliou Niang are not just aggressive but cerebral disruptors on and off the ball.

One weakness has been 3-point shooting. LSU’s starting shooting guard Skyy Clark is 1 of 16 from beyond the arc. The sharpshooter is in a cold spell that the team isn’t worried about. However, besides backup two-guard Abdi Bashir, there aren’t other players who are reliably going to take, let alone make, multiple 3-pointers in a game.

While LSU can be an elite two-point scoring squad, it will be tough to win against strong opponents if Clark and Bashir are missing.

Q: What are a couple of keys for LSU to be successful against Gonzaga?

Brown: One key will be rebounding. LSU hasn’t dominated its lesser competition on the glass enough, specifically defensively. The Tigers have the size to do better, but they’re relying on French center Brice Dessert, who is still adjusting to the pace of the American game.

Giving second-chance scoring opportunities to players like Braden Huff will be much more harmful than it was against Louisiana Tech.

Another key will be the turnover margin. Gonzaga has been exceptional at securing the ball so far. If LSU has a similar number of field goal attempts, Mark Few’s team will win. LSU will use a full-court press to force live-ball turnovers that can grease the wheel of its offense.

Wade won’t expect to force 23 turnovers as it did against Louisiana Tech, so he’ll need his players to be sound decision-makers and value their possessions. Forfeiting easy looks to Gonzaga’s already high-powered offense is a death knell.

Gonzaga.title: Analyzing Gonzaga's 2-0 start, and a look ahead to LSU | Zags Basketball Insiders Podcast
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga has handled Purdue and New Mexico State, but the challenge figures to get tougher Saturday against LSU in the Spokane Veterans Memorial Arena.

Richard Fox and yours truly discussed what we’ve seen from No. 14 Gonzaga thus far and size up the showdown against the 3-0 Tigers in the latest Zags Insiders Podcast.

Find the entire podcast at spokesman.com/podcasts/zags-basketball-insiders/ or YouTube on The Spokesman-Review’s channel. Here are a few excerpts, edited for space considerations.

Early impressions

Fox: We talked about needing some time to understand what this group is. It’s pretty evident, and this is not a surprise because it’s Gonzaga basketball, they’re going to be very good offensively. The first couple games, averaging eight turnovers, assisting on something like 42% of their shots, assisting on makes.

The 3-point shot, 19 of 40, 48%. That’s a really small sample size and I still have PTSD from the last three seasons, but early returns indicate that we’re looking at a team that’s not going to be bad (on 3s).

They put a lot of foul pressure on teams and they’re getting out on the break. The offensive potential is as good as we’ve seen in quite a while.

On the flip side, the defense and rebounding have not been great. Purdue’s (7-foot-4 Daniel) Jacobsen, yes he’s big and they’re very fundamental, but they’re not a big team. New Mexico State doesn’t have high-major size, even though they have some guys that are good and crafty. Gonzaga is just plus-7 in two games on the glass.

Meehan: The best stat of that entire game (vs. NMSU) wasn’t the three players that had 20 points. I don’t even think it was (Xaivian) Lee’s 10 assists. He’s off to a great start. Davis Fogle’s six assists, I think, that’s a very important stat as much as his (22) points.

He’s truly a guy that can create and dish. He’s taking on a lot of the offensive load right now. They do have other guys that can create but he can really create. He can draw the big, he can draw the help from the wing and that maybe is creating some open looks that they’re cashing in on.

Isiah Harwell can shoot it when he is set and his form (is good). When he’s drifting or forcing it or rushing it, that’s a different story.

If Fogle can (create), that can really alleviate (pressure on others). They’ve got capable scorers.

Talking Tigers

Meehan: Somewhere in that top 10 or 15, LSU’s lineup would probably rank there for sure. The Zags will know a few of these guys, (former UCLA guards) Donovan Dent and Skyy Clark.

Dent had that great run at New Mexico and he came along last year (at UCLA) and put up good numbers. He’s legitimately a great college player. Clark is a very good shooter. He hasn’t found it yet (1 of 16 on 3-pointers), but he’s way better than that.

It’s going to be a battle physically. It’s going to be interesting how it is whistled. Massamba Diop has been in foul trouble pretty much every time he’s suited up. The Zags have been putting a lot of foul pressure on people. These are big, athletic kids, some 22- and 23-year old bodies going at it.

If you look at the offensive rebounding category after the game, you’re going to have a pretty good indication of who wins.

Fox: Gonzaga is going to have to rebound at a much higher level than they have to start the year.

LSU has a lot of talent. Just like GU, they have to get all these pieces together. Dent is a high-level guard. He can really control the game. LSU is going to want to play fast.

It’s going to be a real test for (Nathan) De Sousa, (Javon) Bennett, Lee and Gonzaga as a whole to try to corral him. LSU is one of the few teams in the country that I’d be nervous about trying to run with for 40 minutes. I think you want to force them to score over you.

Their European (players), that’s the hard part. You don’t have a lot of film, you don’t necessarily know who they are, even if you’re super dialed into the Euro game. This is going to be a legitimate test.

Gonzaga.title: With sights on Gonzaga-LSU matchup, Chauncey Wiggins has 5-in-5 eligibility hearing moved to Thursday
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga is running a hurry-up offense in its attempt to get Chauncey Wiggins on the court before Saturday’s marquee nonconference matchup with LSU at Numerica Veterans Arena.

The Florida State transfer is now set to appear at an injunction hearing at 1:30 p.m. Thursday before Superior Court Judge Dean Chuang. If granted, the injunction could allow Wiggins to make his Gonzaga debut against the Tigers.

Wiggins was not initially scheduled to have his 5-in-5 eligibility case heard until Nov. 17, eliminating the possibility that he’d suit up in Saturday’s game. Wiggins’ attorneys, Carl Oreskovich and Andrew Wagley of Spokane-based firm Etter, McMahon, Lamberson, Van Wert & Oreskovich, P.C., filed a motion to shorten time that was approved by Spokane Superior Court, bumping the injunction hearing up by five days.

In a motion to shorten time posted to the Spokane Superior Court web docket, Wiggins’ attorneys contest the player will continue to “suffer irreparable harm” with every game missed this season, “particularly primetime games in the national spotlight.” The motion also argued the NCAA will “suffer essentially no harm” if an injunction is granted.

Wiggins dressed in street clothes and didn’t play in both of Gonzaga’s wins last week – a 78-72 victory over Purdue in Las Vegas in the season opener and a 109-68 blowout of New Mexico State on Saturday at McCarthey Athletic Center.

A 6-foot-10 wing who averaged 13.3 points on 38% 3-point shooting last season at Florida State, Wiggins originally joined a group of student-athletes seeking a fifth season of eligibility through the Godfrey vs. NCAA 5-in-5 lawsuit filed in Wiggins’ home state of Georgia. The plaintiffs were successful, earning an injunction that cleared them to compete, but the case was ultimately stayed, reversing the verdict until oral arguments were heard on Jan. 12.

Seeking expedited relief, Wiggins and other plaintiffs refiled in Waco, Texas, joining student-athletes who’d previously received a temporary restraining order in the Wheeler vs. NCAA 5-in-5 case. A judge heard the case four days before Gonzaga’s opener against Purdue, but dismissed the TRO and denied the special appearance, citing “lack of personal jurisdiction.”

Wiggins’ eligibility fight continues in Spokane County, where Oreskovich will represent him. Last October, Oreskovich helped former Gonzaga player Tyon Grant-Foster secure an injunction that allowed Grant-Foster to play for Mark Few’s team in 2025-26. Chuang, who was appointed to the 13th judgeship by then-Gov. Jay Inslee in 2023, is a Walla Walla native who resided in Olympia before attending Gonzaga Law School.

Three declaration affidavits, from Wiggins, Few and Gonzaga Compliance Director Scott Garrison, were also filed to the Superior Court docket on Monday, as was a pro hac vice motion that allows Ryan Downton – Wiggins’ primary attorney in the Georgia and Texas lawsuits – to participate in the lawsuit.

Gonzaga’s coach argued “it is critically important for Mr. Wiggins that he be allowed to compete as soon as possible,” stressing that “each day he misses will postpone his ability to learn the system, mesh with teammates, and ultimately delay his ability to perform in competition games under a national spotlight.”

Gonzaga.title: Unbeaten week moves Gonzaga up one spot to No. 14 in Associated Press poll
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga’s perfect start to the regular season came with a slight bump in Monday’s Associated Press Top 25 poll.

The Zags moved up one spot to No. 14 after narrowly beating Purdue 78-72 in the season opener at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas and cruising for a 109-68 home victory against New Mexico State.

There was no movement inside the top four of the first regular-season Top 25 poll, but 19 of the 21 teams ranked between No. 5 and No. 25 moved up or down at least one spot, with UCLA making the biggest jump of anyone, shooting up 13 spots to No. 9 after an 84-75 victory over former Gonzaga assistant Tommy Lloyd and Arizona in Vegas. The loss also dropped Arizona seven spots to No. 12 in the new poll.

The top 10 consists of No. 1 Florida, No. 2 Duke, No. 3 Illinois, No. 4 UConn, No. 5 Michigan State, No. 6 Virginia, No. 7 Texas, No. 8 Houston, No. 9 UCLA and No. 10 Louisville.

The Zags are positioned to play three top-10 teams – Duke, Michigan State and UCLA – during the nonconference schedule. Seven of Gonzaga’s potential opponents at the Players Era 16 also held down spots in Monday’s poll: No. 10 Louisville, No. 11 Tennessee, No. 13 St. John’s, No. 16 Texas Tech, No. 17 Miami, No. 18 Alabama and No. 20 Michigan.

Four other possible opponents in Vegas – Iowa State, Baylor, TCU and Creighton – another potential second-round opponent in Vegas, received Top 25 votes. The Zags will see Creighton later on, visiting the Bluejays for a Dec. 12 game in Omaha.

Utah State was the only other Pac-12 team to receive a Top 25 vote. The Aggies appeared on one ballot, at No. 25, after opening the season with comfortable wins over Idaho State and Omaha.

Gonzaga didn’t move in Monday’s USA Today Coaches Poll, remaining at No. 12.
